mainTopic: Why one witness is believed that a husband died (ending with רבי זירא and the concern for an עגונה), and רב's limit on the rule that she must leave both men.
overview: The גמרא is looking for the reason one witness (עד אחד) is believed that a woman's husband died, so she may remarry. First it rejects a proof from a case about חלב: there the person brings a קרבן because his silence counts as admitting, not because one witness is believed. Next it tries plain logic, comparing the case to a doubtful piece of meat. It then argues that since two witnesses could free her, one should be believed too, like with טבל, הקדש and קונמות. But it checks each of those examples and finds that the witness is believed only because he could fix the item himself, or else the case has no source of its own. So רבי זירא gives a new reason: because she is punished so harshly if the husband returns, she will check carefully, and the רבנן could be lenient with one witness to keep her from being an עגונה. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's rule that she must leave both men. רב limits that rule to a woman who remarried on one witness, and the case is narrowed to a returning man people don't recognize, with proof from יוסף's brothers. The amud ends with a challenge: in the two-witness case it is two against two, so why may she stay?

steps.title: Why do the רבנן obligate a קרבן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן require a קרבן when one witness says the person ate חלב and he stays silent. It offers a first guess: because the single witness is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason the רבנן obligate him? If you say it is because the witness is believed...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is checking the earlier proof by asking what the real reason is behind the רבנן's ruling. It offers a first guess that it is about trusting the witness, and the next step will test that guess.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier proof only works if the רבנן obligate the קרבן because one witness is trusted. So the גמרא asks for the reason, and the first option it raises is exactly that the witness is believed (מהימן).

keyTerms.meaning: They obligate (here: to bring a קרבן)
If you say (a suggestion the גמרא is about to test)

phrases.english: What is the reason the Rabbis obligate him?
phrases.notes: This is about the earlier case: one witness says he ate חלב, he stays quiet, and he must bring a קרבן.

phrases.english: If you say it is because the witness is believed —

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא קָא מְחַיְּיבִי רַבָּנַן? אִילֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts testing the earlier proof that one witness is believed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the real basis for the רבנן obligating a קרבן on one witness's word?

steps.title: Even two witnesses are not enough when he denies it
steps.stepSummary: If trust in the witness were the reason, it makes no sense: with two witnesses whom he contradicts, the רבנן exempt him from a קרבן even though two witnesses are fully believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But look at a normal pair of witnesses: even though he contradicts them, they are believed, and still the רבנן exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the guess that the רבנן trust one witness. If two fully believed witnesses cannot obligate him when he denies it, one witness surely cannot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two witnesses are the strongest kind of evidence, yet when the person denies their claim the רבנן exempt him from a קרבן. So the קרבן cannot be based on how believable the witnesses are. Something else must be behind the ruling in the silent case.

phrases.english: But there is the case of an ordinary pair of witnesses,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּקָא מַכְחִישׁ לְהוּ אִינְהוּ —
phrases.english: where even though he contradicts them, they —
are believed, and yet the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refutes the suggestion raised in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the רבנן obligate a קרבן because one witness is believed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If two believed witnesses do not obligate a קרבן when he denies it, belief in witnesses cannot be the reason; one witness would be even weaker.

steps.title: The real reason: silence counts as admitting
steps.stepSummary: The קרבן comes because he stayed quiet, and silence is like admitting. So the case proves nothing about believing one witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it because he stayed silent, and silence is like admitting?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the true reason for the רבנן's ruling, and with it the earlier proof falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person brings a קרבן because by not denying it he basically admitted he ate חלב. His own admission obligates him, not the witness. So this case cannot be the source that one witness is believed about a husband's death.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof from the חלב case is rejected: silence counts as admission (שתיקה כהודאה דמיא), so the witness's believability was never the reason.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not because he stayed silent —
and silence is like an admission?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the alternative reason, which closes off the earlier proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the חלב case for believing one witness.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The obligation comes from his silence acting as admission, not from trusting the single witness.

steps.title: It is logic, like a doubtful piece of meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the source is plain logic: just as one witness is believed that a doubtful piece of meat is permitted fat (שומן), he is believed that the husband died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is logic: it is like a piece of meat that might be forbidden fat or might be permitted fat, and one witness comes and says, 'I am sure it is permitted fat.' He is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected the proof from the רבנן's ruling about the silent person, the גמרא now says the rule comes from סברא, comparing it to a known case of one witness resolving a doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a piece of meat is in doubt, one witness who is sure it is שומן is believed. The גמרא suggests the same should apply to a woman whose husband's death is in doubt: one sure witness settles it.

phrases.english: Rather, it is logical reasoning,
just like the case of a piece of meat

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק שֶׁל חֵלֶב סָפֵק שֶׁל שׁוּמָּן,
phrases.english: that may be forbidden fat or may be permitted fat,
and one witness came and said:
'I am sure it is permitted fat' — that he is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא סְבָרָא הִיא, מִידֵּי דְּהָוֵה אַחֲתִיכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the proof, offers a new basis from logic.
steps.raayaObject: That one witness is believed that a husband died.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of a doubtful piece of meat, where one witness is believed that it is שומן.

steps.title: A married woman already has a forbidden status
steps.stepSummary: The comparison fails: the meat never had a known forbidden status, but a married woman is known to be forbidden, and ערוה matters need two witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they really alike? There, no prohibition was ever established. Here, the prohibition of a married woman is established, and nothing involving ערוה can be done with fewer than two witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the comparison from step 4 by pointing out a big difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the meat, we never knew it was forbidden, so one witness can tip the doubt. With the woman, we know for sure she is an אשת איש, a fixed forbidden status (חזקת איסור). On top of that, there is a rule that ערוה matters need two witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? (a challenge to a comparison)
A prohibition has been established (a known forbidden status)

phrases.english: Is it comparable?
There, no prohibition was established,
here, the prohibition of a married woman is established,
and no matter of forbidden relations is decided by fewer than two!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? הָתָם לָא אִיתַּחְזַק אִיסּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the comparison made in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison between the woman and the doubtful piece of meat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The meat had no established prohibition, but the woman has an established prohibition as an אשת איש, and ערוה matters require two witnesses.

steps.title: The better comparison: meat that is surely חלב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the woman's case really matches meat known to be חלב, where one witness saying it is שומן is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is only like a piece of meat that is surely forbidden fat, and one witness comes and says, 'I am sure it was permitted fat.' He is not believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the challenge further by offering a closer comparison, one that points the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the woman has a known forbidden status, the right parallel is meat known to be חלב. There one witness is not believed, so by this logic one witness should not be believed about the husband's death either.

phrases.english: This is only comparable
to a piece that is definitely forbidden fat,
and one witness came and said:

phrases.aramaic: בָּרִי לִי דְּשׁוּמָּן הֲוָה — דְּלָא מְהֵימַן!
phrases.english: 'I am sure it was permitted fat' — where he is not believed!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא לָא דָּמְיָא אֶלָּא לַחֲתִיכָה דְּוַדַּאי חֵלֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 5's challenge by naming the closer, opposite comparison.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that logic supports believing one witness about the husband's death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A case with an established prohibition matches meat that is definitely חלב, where one witness is not believed.

steps.title: If two would be believed, one is believed too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison: with surely-חלב meat even a hundred witnesses cannot change it, but a husband's death can be shown by two witnesses, so one is believed too, like with טבל, הקדש and קונמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it comparable? There, even a hundred witnesses would not be believed. Here, since two witnesses would be believed, let us believe one too, just like with untithed produce, consecrated property and vowed items.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and defends the idea that one witness is believed about the husband's death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat that is truly חלב can never become permitted, so no number of witnesses can help, and the comparison fails. A woman's status can change if her husband dies, as two witnesses could show. When a forbidden status can be changed, one witness is believed, as we see with טבל, הקדש and קונמות.

keyTerms.meaning: Property given to the בית המקדש
Things made forbidden by a vow

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא answers that the woman is not like surely-חלב meat, because two witnesses could change her status. It supports this with טבל, הקדש and קונמות, but the next steps check whether those parallels really hold.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say a married woman lacks a forbidden status. It says her forbidden status can be removed, so one witness can be believed, even though the prohibition was established.
steps.whyThisMatters: This סברא does not end up as the final basis. Steps 8–12 show that טבל, הקדש and קונמות each prove nothing, and the real basis comes from רבי זירא and the concern for an עגונה in steps 13–15.

phrases.english: Is it comparable?

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, אֲפִילּוּ אָתוּ בֵּי מְאָה לָא מְהֵימְנִי.
phrases.english: There, even if a hundred came, they would not be believed.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, כֵּיוָן דְּכִי אָתוּ בֵּי תְרֵי מְהֵימְנִי —
phrases.english: Here, since if two came they would be believed —
let us believe one as well,
just like untithed produce, consecrated property, and vowed items.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? הָתָם, אֲפִילּוּ אָתוּ בֵּי מְאָה לָא מְהֵימְנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 6's comparison and defends the logic of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: a prohibition that can never change versus one that can be removed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A woman with an established prohibition is like meat that is surely חלב, so one witness is not believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since two witnesses could remove her prohibition, one witness is believed too, as with טבל, הקדש and קונמות.

steps.title: What exactly is the case of untithed produce?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose טבל the witness is talking about. If it is his own, he is believed only because he can tithe it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: This טבל, what is the case? If it is his own, he is believed because he has the power to fix it. So it must be someone else's. Then what does this opinion hold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to take apart the טבל example from step 7. It asks whose produce the witness is talking about, and this sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the produce is the witness's own, he is believed because he could tithe it right now anyway. That is a special reason (בידו) which a witness about a dead husband does not have. So the case must be about someone else's produce, and the גמרא now asks what rule applies there.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce from which תרומה and מעשרות have not yet been taken; forbidden to eat
What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
Because it is in his hands, meaning he has the power to do it himself
To fix it, here by taking off the tithes so the food becomes permitted

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying one witness is never believed about טבל. It is saying the reason he is believed may be special to that case (בידו), so it cannot prove anything about a woman's husband.

phrases.english: This untithed produce, what is the case?
If it is his own,
he is believed because it is in his power to fix it.
Rather, it is someone else's. Then what does he hold?
phrases.notes: 'He' means whoever brought the טבל example in step 7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts checking the טבל example used in step 7's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose טבל is the witness testifying about, his own or someone else's?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: If it is his own, he is believed because of בידו. The case of someone else's produce is examined in the next step.

steps.title: Someone else's produce gives no real source
steps.stepSummary: If anyone may tithe for another without the owner's consent, the witness is again believed because of בידו. If consent is needed, and he simply says 'I know it was tithed,' we have no source that he is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he holds that one who separates tithes from his own produce for his friend's produce does not need the owner's consent, then the witness is believed because he could fix it himself. And if he holds that the owner's consent is needed, and the witness says, 'I know about it that it was fixed,' then where do we learn that very rule from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge on the טבל example. Either the witness has his own power to fix the produce, or the case is just as unproven as our case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two possible views about tithing someone else's produce. If no consent is needed, the witness can tithe it himself, so he is believed because of בידו, which does not help our case. If consent is needed, he has no such power, and why he is believed is exactly what we are trying to prove. So it cannot be used as a source.

keyTerms.meaning: One who separates תרומה (the gift for the כהן)
That itself, from where do we know it? (The case you brought needs a source too.)

steps.whatToRemember: For טבל: either the witness is believed because he can fix it himself, or there is no source at all. Either way it does not prove one witness is believed about a husband's death.

phrases.aramaic: אִי קָא סָבַר: תּוֹרֵם מִשֶּׁלּוֹ עַל שֶׁל חֲבֵרוֹ
phrases.english: If he holds: one who separates tithes from his own produce for his friend's produce
does not need the owner's consent,
then he is believed because it is in his power to fix it.
And if he holds: the owner's consent is needed,
and the witness says: I know about it that it was fixed,
that very thing, from where do we know it?
phrases.notes: Meaning: this case is no clearer than the case of the woman, so it cannot be her source.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'what does he hold' question from step 8 and turns it into a challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of טבל in step 7 as a source that one witness is believed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Either the witness has the power to tithe the produce himself (בידו), which does not apply to a husband's death, or the rule that he is believed has no source of its own.

steps.title: The same problem with consecrated property
steps.stepSummary: With הקדש, the witness is believed because of בידו, either because he can redeem it or because he can have his vow undone. If it is someone else's, there is no source.
steps.simpleTranslation: Consecrated property too. If it has holiness of value, he is believed because he has the power to redeem it. If it has holiness of the body itself: if it is his own, he is believed because he has the power to ask a חכם to undo the vow. Rather, it is someone else's, and he says, 'I know about it that its owner asked to undo it.' Then where do we learn that very rule from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now runs the same challenge on the הקדש example from step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the item only has value-holiness, he can redeem it, so he is believed because of בידו. If it has body-holiness (like an animal for a קרבן) and it is his own, he can go to a חכם to undo the vow, which is again בידו. If it is someone else's, he has no such power, and why he is believed still needs a source.

keyTerms.meaning: Property dedicated to the בית המקדש
Holiness of value: only the item's worth is holy, so it can be redeemed
Holiness of the body: the item itself is holy, like an animal for a קרבן
To ask a חכם to undo a vow (שאלה על נדר)

phrases.english: Consecrated property too: if it has holiness of value,
he is believed because it is in his power to redeem it.
If it has holiness of the body itself: if it is his own,
he is believed because it is in his power to ask to have it undone.
Rather, it is someone else's, and he says:
I know about it that its owner asked to have it undone,
that very thing, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same two-sided challenge from step 9 to the second example, הקדש.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of הקדש in step 7 as a source that one witness is believed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In every version of הקדש that belongs to the witness, he could permit it himself (redeem it or undo the vow). If it belongs to someone else, there is no source that he is believed.

steps.title: The same problem with קונמות
steps.stepSummary: With קונמות, the witness is believed because he can redeem the item, if it has value-holiness. If it is only a plain prohibition and the item is his own, he is believed because he can have the vow undone.
steps.simpleTranslation: קונמות too. If he holds there is מעילה with קונמות, and holiness of value comes upon them, then he is believed because he has the power to redeem it. And if he holds there is no מעילה with קונמות, and it is just a prohibition riding on its shoulders: if it is his own, he is believed because he has the power to ask a חכם to undo the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same challenge to the third example, קונמות. It does this for both views of what kind of holiness a קונם has.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a קונם is treated like הקדש (it has מעילה and value-holiness), it can be redeemed, so the witness is believed because of בידו. If it is only a plain prohibition and the item is the witness's own, he can have the vow undone, which is again בידו. The case of someone else's item, where he has no such power, is the step the גמרא takes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Items forbidden by a vow, using the word קונם ('this is forbidden to me like a קרבן')
The sin of using holy property for ordinary purposes
Just a plain prohibition, with no real holiness

phrases.english: קונמות too: if he holds:
there is מעילה with קונמות,
and holiness of value comes upon them,
then he is believed because it is in his power to redeem it.
And if he holds: there is no מעילה with קונמות,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיסּוּר בְּעָלְמָא הוּא דְּרָכֵיב לְהוּ אַכַּתְפֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: and it is just a prohibition riding on its shoulders,
then if it is his own,
he is believed because it is in his power to ask to have it undone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same challenge to the third example, קונמות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of קונמות in step 7 as a source that one witness is believed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under either view of a קונם, if the item is the witness's own, he could permit it himself (redeem it or undo the vow). So the case gives no source for believing a witness who has no such power.

steps.title: The last comparison fails, so the original question is back
steps.stepSummary: If the קונם belongs to someone else and the witness only says 'I know the owner had his vow undone,' we have no source that he is believed. So we still don't know why one witness is believed about a husband's death.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the item belongs to someone else, and the witness says 'I know its owner had his vow undone,' then for that very case, where do we learn that he is believed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its attack on the קונמות comparison by looking at a case where the item belongs to someone else. With that, every proof has failed, and the original question is open again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier cases the witness was believed only because he could fix things himself (בידו). Here he has no such power, since it is not his item and not his vow. That is exactly like the husband case, and for this case we have no source at all. So the comparisons prove nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: had a vow undone by asking a חכם
this case itself, where do we know it from?

steps.whatToRemember: All the comparisons (טבל, הקדש, קונמות) only work because of בידו, so none of them explains why one witness is believed about a husband's death.

phrases.english: Rather, if it belongs to someone else,
and he says: I know
that its owner had the vow on it undone —
this case itself, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes step 11's breakdown of the קונמות case by covering the case where the item belongs to someone else.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 7 that one witness is believed about a husband's death just as he is with טבל, הקדש and קונמות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Those cases only work because of בידו. In the case that truly matches the husband case, where the witness has no power to act, there is no source that one witness is believed.

steps.title: רבי זירא: strict at the end, so lenient at the start
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that because the woman is punished so harshly if the husband turns up alive, the רבנן could accept one witness to let her remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Because of the strictness you placed on her at the end, you were lenient with her at the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא gives a new answer to why an עד אחד is believed, one that does not depend on comparisons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the husband comes back, the woman suffers severe penalties. Because she knows this, she will check carefully before remarrying on one witness's word. That built-in caution is what makes it safe to accept just one witness at the start.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who gives the new answer

steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the basic reason why one witness is enough for a woman to remarry.

phrases.english: רבי זירא said:
Because of the strictness
that you placed on her at the end —
phrases.notes: 'The end' means if her husband turns up alive and she gets the משנה's harsh penalties.

phrases.english: you were lenient with her at the beginning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question left open in step 12 with a new kind of reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reasoning that replaces the failed comparisons
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought one witness had to be believed because of a parallel case like טבל or הקדש.
steps.terutzMaskana: One witness is believed because the harsh penalty for being wrong makes the woman check carefully.

steps.title: Why not skip both the strictness and the leniency?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why not simply require two witnesses and drop the harsh penalties?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us not be strict and not be lenient!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי זירא's answer: if the strictness exists only to allow the leniency, why not do away with both?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual rule is two witnesses, which needs no extra penalties. Creating a leniency and then adding harsh penalties to balance it seems pointless when we could just keep the normal rule.

phrases.english: Let us not be strict and not be lenient!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי זירא's answer in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's reasoning that the strictness at the end allows leniency at the start.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the two cancel out, it would be simpler to keep the normal two-witness rule with no penalties.

steps.title: The leniency is to prevent an עגונה
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן were lenient so the woman would not be stuck as an עגונה, unable to remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the concern of a woman being left chained, the רבנן were lenient with her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the leniency is needed at all: without it, many women could never remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is often hard to find two witnesses to a husband's death. Without accepting one witness, the woman would stay chained forever. So the leniency is truly needed, and the strictness keeps it from being misused.

keyTerms.meaning: the state of being an עגונה, a woman chained to a missing husband

steps.whatToRemember: One witness is believed because of עגונה concerns, and the harsh penalties make sure the woman checks carefully.
steps.whyThisMatters: The concern for an עגונה drives many leniencies in these laws.

phrases.english: Because of the concern of her being chained
the רבנן were lenient with her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the practical need behind the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The leniency and the strictness cancel out, so both could be dropped.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency is needed so women are not chained, and the strictness protects it.

steps.title: רב: she must leave both only if she married on one witness
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה's rule that she must leave both men, רב says this applies only when she remarried on one witness, not on two.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says she must leave this one and this one. רב said: They only taught this when she married based on one witness, but if she married based on two witnesses, she does not have to leave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the משנה's rule that the woman must leave both husbands, and רב narrows when it applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's harsh rule applies when she relied on a single witness. According to רב, if two witnesses testified that the husband died, she does not have to leave her second husband.

keyTerms.meaning: she must leave this one and that one, meaning both husbands
they taught this only in the case of

phrases.english: She must leave this one and this one, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה, about a woman who remarried and then her first husband came back.

phrases.english: רב said: They taught this only
when she married based on one witness,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל נִיסֵּת עַל פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים — לֹא תֵּצֵא.
phrases.english: but if she married based on two witnesses, she does not leave.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּיסֵּת בְּעֵד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה, about what happens when the husband comes back.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule that she must leave both applies only when she remarried on one witness. With two witnesses, she stays with the second husband.

steps.title: ארץ ישראל laughs: the husband is standing right here!
steps.stepSummary: The scholars in ארץ ישראל mocked רב's ruling. The husband has come back alive, so how can she stay with the second man?
steps.simpleTranslation: They laughed at him in the West: The man has come and is standing here, and you say she does not have to leave?
steps.whatsHappening: The scholars of ארץ ישראל attack רב's ruling as clearly wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the first husband is alive and standing before us, the witnesses were obviously wrong. Her second marriage was never valid, no matter how many witnesses there were.

keyTerms.meaning: in the West, meaning ארץ ישראל
the man, here the first husband

phrases.english: They laughed at him in the West:
phrases.notes: 'The West' is how the Babylonian גמרא refers to ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: The man has come and is standing here,
and you say she does not leave?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's ruling in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that with two witnesses she does not have to leave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The living husband in front of us proves the witnesses wrong, so her second marriage cannot stand.

steps.title: רב means a case where we don't recognize the man
steps.stepSummary: רב's ruling is needed for a case where we do not know whether the man claiming to be her husband really is.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where we do not recognize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by explaining which case he means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב is not talking about a husband we clearly recognize. He means a stranger who claims to be her husband. Against two witnesses who said the husband died, his claim alone does not force her to leave.

keyTerms.meaning: it is only needed for (a specific case)

steps.whatToRemember: רב's ruling covers only a man we cannot identify. If the husband is clearly recognized, she must leave.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where we do not recognize him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the mockery in step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב was talking about a husband everyone recognizes.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב means a man whose identity is unknown, so the two witnesses still stand.

steps.title: If we don't know him, why must she leave even with one witness?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges step 18: if this man's identity is unknown, why should she leave in the case of one witness?
steps.simpleTranslation: If we do not know whether he is really her husband, then why should she have to leave when she remarried on one witness?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 18. If we cannot tell whether this man is really the husband, then even a woman who remarried on one witness should not have to leave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עד אחד who says the husband died is normally trusted so the woman can remarry. A stranger who merely claims to be the husband does not contradict that witness. So why does רב make her leave in the one-witness case?

phrases.english: If we do not know him,
phrases.notes: He means we can't tell whether this man is really her husband, which is the case from step 18.

phrases.english: why should she leave when it was one witness?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דְּלָא יָדְעִינַן לֵיהּ, בְּעֵד אֶחָד אַמַּאי תֵּצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case setting proposed in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 18 that רב's ruling deals with a man of unknown identity.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his identity is unknown, nothing contradicts the עד אחד, so the difference between one witness and two disappears.

steps.title: Two people say they were with him the whole time
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where two witnesses say they stayed with the man since he left, so he is the husband. We just don't recognize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ruling is needed where two people came and said: We were with him from when he left until now, and you are the ones who don't recognize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by making the case more specific. Two witnesses come and say this really is the husband. They were with him the whole time, and he only looks different now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is real testimony that he is alive. Against one witness who said he died, two witnesses win, so she must leave. When she remarried on two witnesses, it becomes two against two, and רב says she does not have to leave.

keyTerms.meaning: it is only needed for (this specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where two came and said:
We were with him
from when he left until now,
and it is you who do not recognize him,

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דַּאֲתוֹ בֵּי תְרֵי וְאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Unknown identity means nobody contradicts the witness of death, so even with one witness she could stay.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two witnesses vouch that he is the husband. This beats one witness of death, so she leaves, but not when she remarried on two witnesses.

steps.title: Proof from יוסף that a person's looks can change
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק and רב חסדא's teaching show that someone can grow unrecognizable, even to his own brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And יוסף recognized his brothers but they did not recognize him.' רב חסדא said: This teaches that he left without a full beard and came back with a full beard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the claim that the people at home simply don't recognize him. Even יוסף's own brothers did not recognize him after years apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא explains why the brothers failed: יוסף left before his beard had grown in, and they met him again with a full beard. So it is believable that a returning husband is real even though people don't recognize him.

phrases.english: as it is written:
"And Joseph recognized his brothers
but they did not recognize him",
and Rav Chisda said:
this teaches that he left without a full beard,
and came with a full beard.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: וַיַּכֵּר יוֹסֵף אֶת אֶחָיו וְהֵם לֹא הִכִּירוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim in step 20 that the husband could be real but unrecognized.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a man can change so much that people who knew him don't recognize him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 42:8 as explained by רב חסדא: יוסף left without a full beard and returned with one.

steps.title: In the end it is two witnesses against two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the two-witness case: two said he died and two say he is alive, so why may she stay?
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, it is two witnesses against two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. In the case where she remarried on two witnesses, two say he died and two say this is him alive. Why should she get to stay with the second man?
steps.deeperAnalysis: When two עדים contradict two עדים, neither pair beats the other, so the situation stays in doubt. A doubt like this should not let her stay married to the second man, so רב's ruling seems hard to understand.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a final ruling that she must leave. The גמרא is raising a problem with רב's view and will answer it next.

phrases.english: In the end, they are two against two,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the outcome produced by the answer in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that she does not leave when she remarried on two witnesses, in the case set up in step 20.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two witnesses of death against two witnesses of life cancel each other out and leave a doubt, so why may she stay with the second husband?
